scenes.title: The onboarding bottleneck
scenes.narration: From the outside, Ahsha's bottleneck looks like going live, not selling. Public posts mention contracted revenue piling up, and more demand than the team can onboard. My guess is that every new practice needs someone to turn its scripts, hours, provider lists and protocols into agent settings by hand. This prototype tests that guess. It compiles a practice's intake packet into an agent konfig, checks it, and leaves a person only the exceptions.

My guess is that every new practice needs someone to turn its scripts, hours, provider lists and protocols into agent settings by hand.
This prototype tests that guess.
It compiles a practice's intake packet into an agent konfig, checks it, and leaves a person only the exceptions.

scenes.title: Architecture
scenes.narration: Plain code handles anything that must be exact and repeatable. The compiler parses five packet files into a typed konfig. The validator runs nine deterministic rules. A semantic check looks for an F-A-Q answer that contradicts the call script. That is the only place a language model is allowed. Each issue then gets a proposed fix. After that come review, a smoke test, and a gated export.

scenes.title: Synthetic packets with an answer key
scenes.narration: There's no real practice data anywhere. A seeded generator writes six fake practices: internal medicine, cardiology, pulmonology, urgent care and a multispecialty group. Each packet ships a defects file, the answer key for the mistakes planted in it. Thirty in total, and one practice is deliberately clean, to catch false alarms. A test regenerates everything and fails if the committed data has drifted.

scenes.title: Trace: compiling practice three
scenes.narration: Let's follow one practice, Harborview Heart Clinic, a cardiology packet. Load packet reads the five files as lines, and compile packet walks them. Line twelve of the hours file says Friday, eight to three. A pattern match finds the day, parse time converts the times to twenty-four hour form, and the result is a day-hours object with the source hours dot T-X-T, colon twelve. Pie-dantic requires a source on every item, and checks its format.

scenes.title: Trace: checking practice three
scenes.narration: Now the compiled konfig goes to run rules. Take the hours conflict rule. It scans every line the agent might say, script lines and F-A-Q answers, for phrases like "our Friday hours are". Line nine of the script says eight to five. The official hours say eight to three. So it raises a high-severity issue, and cites both lines as evidence. For this practice the checks raise seven issues, matching its seven planted defects.

scenes.title: The semantic check and its fallback
scenes.narration: The contradiction check has two back ends with the same output. If an L-L-M model is configured and Lite L-L-M is installed, it asks the model for contradictions as Jason. That reply is validated, and every cited line must exist. If anything fails, it falls back to a keyword mock. The mock runs whenever no model is set, so nothing needs a key or a network.

scenes.title: Repair with confidence gating
scenes.narration: Next, the repairer proposes a fix for every issue, with a confidence score and the lines it was drawn from. A fix is applied automatically only when confidence is at least zero point eight, and never for escalation. For Harborview, the Friday hours and the duplicate visit type are fixed automatically. The missing chest-pain rule scores exactly zero point eight, but it's escalation, so it waits for a person, along with four others.

scenes.title: Review, smoke test and gated export
scenes.narration: Reviewer decisions, accept, edit or reject, are stored in SQLite, and replayed on top of the compiled konfig. Then a smoke test sends ten scripted patient messages through a keyword router that reads only that konfig. Harborview passes nine. The chest-pain message finds no rule, so nothing escalates. And export stays blocked while any high-severity issue is open. Here, that's the chest-pain rule and a broken phone number.

scenes.title: Run the demo
scenes.narration: To try it, run make demo, and open localhost, port eight thousand. It needs no keys, no Node, and no network. There are four screens. Practices, with status and open exceptions. Packet to konfig, where clicking a field highlights its source line. Exceptions, with evidence, the proposed fix, and its confidence. And the smoke test, with the export button.

scenes.title: Evaluation and limits
scenes.narration: Make ee-val scores everything against the answer key. In mock mode, the checks find all thirty planted defects, with no false alarms. All twenty-four scored fixes match the known answer, and ninety-five percent of fields need no review. Before review, fifty-seven of sixty smoke tests pass. The three failures are escalation fixes it won't apply alone. These numbers are optimistic, because the defects and the checks were written together. Other limits: the packet format is a guess, the red-flag lists need a physician's review, and the router matches keywords; it isn't a live agent.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.narration: So, to recap. The compiler is deterministic, and every value points back to a file and a line. Nine rules and one semantic check turn mistakes into issues with evidence. Confident fixes apply themselves; escalation always waits for a person. And the answer key lets make ee-val score all of it.
